context: The columns are labeled “Character” and “Unicode.” From top to bottom, the seven characters spell Hello算法 with no spaces. The table reproduces the 16-bit binary values and gives their hexadecimal equivalents.
description: For the English letters in the first five rows, the high 8 bits are padded with 00000000 in gray, and the low 8 bits hold the original code point. A brace on the right labels these rows “1-byte English characters (high bits padded with 0).” A brace beside the last two rows, 算 and 法, labels them “2-byte Chinese characters.”

frames.explanation: If 1-byte English code points and 2-byte Chinese code points were stored together as they are, two consecutive bytes could be misread as either one Chinese character or two English letters. Padding with zeros gives each character in this example 2 bytes, so the string can be split at fixed intervals. The five English letters then take up twice as much space as in ASCII.
frames.title: Code points in Hello算法 shown in 16 bits

result: This 16-bit illustration covers only the example characters, all in the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP). Unicode defines code points up to U+10FFFF, which requires 21 bits. The actual byte count depends on the encoding, such as UTF-8 or UTF-16. Characters do not all occupy a fixed 2 bytes.
summary: Writing the English and Chinese characters at the same 16-bit width shows both the convenience and the cost of fixed-width storage.
